query: What HTTP status code indicates that the client has sent too many requests within a given time, and what header indicates how long to wait?

ground_truth.concept: HTTP Rate Limiting Specification
key_facts: Status code is 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After header indicates how long to wait before making a new request
Retry-After can be specified in seconds or as an HTTP-date

query: What security risk does TLS 1.3 0-RTT Early Data introduce, and how does the protocol mitigate it?

ground_truth.concept: TLS 1.3 0-RTT Replay Attack Mechanics
ground_truth.authoritative_source: IETF RFC 8446 (The Transport Layer Security Protocol Version 1.3)
key_facts: 0-RTT Early Data is vulnerable to replay attacks because it lacks forward secrecy before handshake completion
An attacker can intercept and re-transmit 0-RTT request data to the server
Mitigations include single-use tickets, server ticket age verification, client hello recording, or restricting 0-RTT to idempotent requests

query: Explain the internal object structure and cryptographic hashing used in a Git commit object.

ground_truth.concept: Git Object Storage and Merkle DAG Structure
key_facts: Commit object contains a tree pointer (root directory SHA), parent commit SHA(s), author metadata, committer metadata, and commit message
Historically hashed with SHA-1 (160-bit), modern Git supports SHA-256 (256-bit)
Forms an immutable directed acyclic graph (Merkle DAG)

query: What is the function and default duration of the TCP TIME_WAIT state in RFC 9293?

ground_truth.concept: TCP TIME_WAIT Lifecycle and Purpose
key_facts: TIME_WAIT ensures the remote endpoint has received the final ACK closing the connection
Prevents delayed duplicate segments from an old connection from interfering with a new incarnation on the same 4-tuple
Default duration is 2 * MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime), traditionally 60 to 120 seconds

query: What is the purpose of the PostgreSQL Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and how do checkpoints prevent unbounded recovery time?

ground_truth.concept: PostgreSQL WAL and Checkpointing Architecture
ground_truth.authoritative_source: PostgreSQL Documentation (Reliability and the Write-Ahead Log)
key_facts: WAL records all changes to disk before data pages are updated in shared buffers, providing ACID durability
Checkpoints periodically flush all dirty data pages from shared buffers to disk and write a checkpoint record to WAL
During crash recovery, replay only needs to start from the last checkpoint REDO record rather than the beginning of WAL

query: How does the Raft consensus algorithm resolve split-vote scenarios during leader election?

ground_truth.concept: Raft Consensus Leader Election and Randomized Timeouts
ground_truth.authoritative_source: Ongaro & Ousterhout (In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, USENIX ATC 2014)
key_facts: Split votes happen when multiple followers become candidates simultaneously and divide votes equally
Raft uses randomized election timeouts (typically 150-300ms) to break the symmetry
The candidate with the shortest timeout will time out first, increment the term, and request votes before others

query: How does HTTP/2 HPACK header compression work, and how does it prevent CRIME attacks?

ground_truth.concept: HPACK Header Compression and Security Mitigation
ground_truth.authoritative_source: IETF RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)
key_facts: HPACK maintains a static table of 61 common header fields and an evicting dynamic table of negotiated header fields
Header values can be encoded with static Huffman coding
To prevent CRIME/BREACH compression side-channel attacks, sensitive headers (like cookies or authorization) can be flagged Never-Indexed

query: How does the HyperLogLog algorithm estimate distinct set cardinality and what is its standard error rate?

ground_truth.concept: HyperLogLog Probabilistic Cardinality Estimation
ground_truth.authoritative_source: Flajolet et al. (HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm, 2007)
key_facts: Hashes stream items and observes the maximum number of leading zeros in the hash suffix across m registers
Uses the harmonic mean of 2^(leading zeros) across registers to reduce susceptibility to outliers
Standard error is approximately 1.04 / sqrt(m), requiring minimal memory (e.g. 12 KB for 16,384 registers in Redis)

query: Explain the technical trade-offs between write amplification, read amplification, and space amplification in LSM-tree compaction strategies (Leveled vs Size-Tiered).

ground_truth.concept: LSM-Tree Compaction Amplification Trade-Offs
key_facts: Write amplification measures physical bytes written to storage per logical byte updated
Size-Tiered compaction optimizes for low write amplification but suffers from high space amplification (up to 100%) and higher read amplification
Leveled compaction bounds space amplification (typically ~10%) and reduces read amplification by guaranteeing at most one SST per key per level, but incurs higher write amplification

query: How does the Linux eBPF in-kernel verifier enforce memory safety and prevent kernel panics?

ground_truth.concept: Linux Kernel eBPF Static Verification Engine
key_facts: Performs static control-flow graph (CFG) analysis to verify that program is a DAG with bounded execution (no infinite loops)
Simulates instruction execution to track register state, value ranges, and types (scalar vs pointer)
Enforces bounds checking on all pointer dereferences to prevent out-of-bounds kernel memory reads/writes
Prohibits uninitialized memory access and guarantees program termination

query: Why is the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol considered blocking during coordinator failure, and how does Three-Phase Commit (3PC) address this?

ground_truth.concept: Atomic Distributed Commitment: 2PC vs 3PC
key_facts: In 2PC, if the coordinator crashes after participants have voted YES (prepared) but before sending COMMIT, participants must wait indefinitely holding resource locks
3PC splits the commit decision into PreCommit, ensuring that participants never commit until all participants have acknowledged prepare
3PC allows operational participants to elect a new coordinator and safely timeout to abort or commit without blocking under crash-stop assumptions

query: How does zero-copy data transfer using the Linux sendfile() syscall avoid context switches and user-space memory copies?

ground_truth.concept: Operating System Zero-Copy I/O Pipelines
key_facts: Traditional read/write requires copying data from kernel page cache to user-space buffer and back to socket kernel buffer (4 context switches, 4 data copies)
sendfile() transfers data directly from page cache to the target socket file descriptor within kernel space
With DMA scatter-gather hardware support, data is transferred directly from page cache to network interface without CPU copying

query: Compare the technical trade-offs between HNSW graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search and IVF-PQ vector indexing.

ground_truth.concept: Vector Indexing: Graph-Based HNSW vs Quantized Inverted File (IVF-PQ)
ground_truth.authoritative_source: Malkov & Yashunin (HNSW 2018) / Jegou et al. (Product Quantization 2011)
key_facts: HNSW constructs a multi-layer proximity graph offering state-of-the-art query recall and low query latency, but requires substantial RAM to store raw vectors and graph edges
IVF-PQ clusters the vector space with inverted lists (IVF) and compresses vectors into compact byte codes via Product Quantization (PQ)
IVF-PQ reduces memory footprint by 8x-32x and supports massive billions-scale datasets, at the cost of lower recall and training overhead

query: How does consistent hashing with virtual nodes prevent data skew and hotspotting when nodes join or leave a cluster?

ground_truth.concept: Consistent Hashing and Virtual Node Distribution
ground_truth.authoritative_source: Karger et al. (Consistent Hashing 1997) / DeCandia et al. (Dynamo 2007)
key_facts: In basic consistent hashing, non-uniform random placement of nodes on the hash ring causes high variance in partition range sizes
Virtual nodes (vnodes) assign each physical node multiple distinct positions (e.g. 128-256 tokens) across the ring
When a node joins or leaves, the load is uniformly distributed across all remaining nodes rather than overwhelming the immediate successor

query: Explain the two phases of the classic Paxos consensus algorithm (Prepare/Promise and Accept/Accepted) for reaching agreement on a single value.

ground_truth.concept: Single-Decree Paxos Protocol Mechanics
ground_truth.authoritative_source: Lamport (The Part-Time Parliament 1998 / Paxos Made Simple 2001)
key_facts: Phase 1a (Prepare): Proposer selects proposal number n and sends Prepare(n) to a majority of acceptors
Phase 1b (Promise): Acceptors promise not to accept any future proposals numbered < n, returning the highest-numbered proposal already accepted (if any)
Phase 2a (Accept): Proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value of the highest-numbered proposal in promises or a new value
Phase 2b (Accepted): Acceptors accept the proposal unless they have already promised a higher proposal number

query: How do Linux memory overcommit modes (vm.overcommit_memory 0, 1, 2) work and what criteria does the OOM killer use to select a process to terminate?

ground_truth.concept: Linux Virtual Memory Overcommit and Out-Of-Memory Killer
key_facts: vm.overcommit_memory=0 uses heuristic overcommit algorithm (default)
vm.overcommit_memory=1 always allows overcommit without checking available memory
vm.overcommit_memory=2 enforces strict limit: CommitLimit = Swap + (RAM * overcommit_ratio)
OOM killer computes oom_score based on percentage of RAM/swap consumed, adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 to +1000)

query: Compare gRPC vs REST with JSON for low-latency internal microservice communication in terms of serialization overhead, streaming, and multiplexing.

ground_truth.concept: RPC vs REST Microservice Communication Protocols
ground_truth.authoritative_source: gRPC / Protocol Buffers & HTTP/2 Architecture Specs
key_facts: gRPC utilizes binary Protocol Buffers encoding, reducing serialization overhead and payload size compared to textual JSON
gRPC runs natively over HTTP/2 providing connection multiplexing, flow control, and full duplex bidirectional streaming
REST over HTTP/1.1 requires separate connections or head-of-line blocking, but offers ubiquitous browser compatibility and human-readable debugging

query: Compare Apache Flink vs Apache Spark Structured Streaming for real-time event stream processing architectures.

ground_truth.concept: Stream Processing Architectures: Flink vs Spark Streaming
ground_truth.authoritative_source: Apache Flink & Apache Spark Official Documentation
key_facts: Flink is a native pipelined event-at-a-time streaming engine with sub-second latencies (milliseconds)
Spark Structured Streaming is historically micro-batch driven, providing high throughput for analytics at slightly higher latency (tens to hundreds of ms)
Flink uses Chandy-Lamport distributed asynchronous checkpointing for exact once state, whereas Spark relies on write-ahead logs and RDD lineage replay

query: Compare SQLite Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode vs Rollback Journal mode for concurrent read-heavy and write-heavy workloads.

ground_truth.concept: SQLite Transaction Logging Modes: WAL vs Rollback Journal
key_facts: Rollback journal locks the entire database exclusively during writes, completely blocking concurrent readers
WAL mode appends changes to a separate -wal file, allowing multiple concurrent readers to read unaffected database pages while a writer writes
WAL requires periodic checkpointing and shared memory (-shm file), and does not work over networked filesystems (NFS/CIFS)

query: Compare ClickHouse vs Snowflake for real-time analytical event clickstream querying and data ingestion.

ground_truth.concept: Analytical Data Platforms: ClickHouse vs Snowflake
key_facts: ClickHouse is an open-source columnar DBMS optimized for ultra-high ingest rates (millions of rows/sec) and real-time low-latency analytical aggregations on bare-metal or cloud
Snowflake is a fully managed cloud data warehouse featuring decoupled compute and cloud storage (S3/GCS/Blob)
ClickHouse excels at sub-second telemetry and clickstream dashboards; Snowflake excels at multi-departmental BI, semi-structured queries, and elastic auto-scaling

query: Compare NGINX vs Envoy proxy for modern cloud-native service mesh architectures.

ground_truth.concept: Cloud-Native Proxies: NGINX vs Envoy Proxy
key_facts: NGINX is a high-performance event-driven web server and reverse proxy with traditional static configuration files or commercial reload APIs
Envoy is designed from inception as a service mesh sidecar proxy with dynamic control plane APIs (xDS for listeners, routes, clusters, endpoints)
Envoy provides native out-of-the-box support for distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), gRPC transcoding, and L7 filter pipelines

query: Compare Cap'n Proto vs Protocol Buffers for inter-process communication latency and zero-copy serialization.

ground_truth.concept: Binary Serialization Formats: Cap'n Proto vs Protobuf
ground_truth.authoritative_source: Cap'n Proto & Protocol Buffers Technical Documentation
key_facts: Cap'n Proto formats data in memory identically to its wire format, completely eliminating the encode/decode step (true zero-copy)
Protocol Buffers encodes values with variable-length integers (varints) and nested tags, requiring CPU cycles to pack and parse into language objects
Cap'n Proto trades slightly larger wire payload sizes for zero-CPU serialization and sub-microsecond IPC latency

query: Compare CockroachDB vs TiDB for distributed ACID SQL databases with horizontal scaling and Raft consensus.

ground_truth.concept: Distributed NewSQL Relational Databases: CockroachDB vs TiDB
key_facts: CockroachDB implements Multi-Raft across range partitions, embeds the storage engine (Pebble) in every node, and uses the PostgreSQL wire protocol
TiDB separates compute (TiDB stateless SQL servers) from storage (TiKV distributed transactional key-value cluster running Raft), using MySQL wire protocol
Both provide serializable/snapshot isolation and automatic range splitting, but differ in compute/storage decoupling and protocol compatibility

query: Compare Prometheus pull-based metrics collection vs InfluxDB push-based telemetry for distributed system observability.

ground_truth.concept: Telemetry Ingestion Models: Prometheus Pull vs InfluxDB Push
key_facts: Prometheus uses a pull model where the server periodically scrapes /metrics HTTP endpoints discovered via service discovery (Kubernetes/Consul)
InfluxDB uses a push model where applications or edge agents (Telegraf) stream metrics directly over HTTP/UDP to the database
Pull models simplify target health monitoring and prevent server overload; push models handle short-lived batch jobs and ephemeral serverless functions more naturally

query: Calculate the Return on Investment (ROI) and total net profit for an infrastructure migration costing $200,000 upfront that saves $65,000 annually over a 4-year period.

ground_truth.formula: Total Savings = Annual Savings * Years; Net Profit = Total Savings - Upfront Cost; ROI = (Net Profit / Upfront Cost) * 100

query: Calculate the theoretical maximum speedup under Amdahl's Law for a software program where 80% of execution time is parallelizable running on 16 cores and on 64 cores.
Calculate the Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) in megabytes and optimal TCP window size for a 10 Gbps transatlantic network link with a round-trip time (RTT) of 75 milliseconds.
Calculate the total training FLOPs required to pre-train a 7-billion parameter transformer model on 2 trillion tokens using the standard compute approximation (6 * P * D).
Calculate the Net Revenue Retention (NRR) percentage for a SaaS business starting at $1,000,000 ARR with $120,000 expansion, $30,000 contraction, and $40,000 churn.

ground_truth.formula: Ending ARR = Starting ARR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn; NRR = (Ending ARR / Starting ARR) * 100

query: Calculate the total raw storage requirement in gigabytes for 100 million sensor telemetry records with 128 bytes payload, 32 bytes metadata overhead per record, and 3x cluster replication.

ground_truth.formula: Record Size = Payload + Overhead; Unreplicated Bytes = Records * Record Size; Total Replicated Bytes = Unreplicated Bytes * 3; Storage GB = Replicated Bytes / 10^9 (or 1024^3)

ground_truth.challenge: False Premise: HTTP/1.1 is claimed to be faster and more efficient than HTTP/3 on lossy networks
ground_truth.expected_behavior: System must explicitly challenge and correct the premise, explaining that HTTP/1.1 suffers from TCP Head-of-Line blocking and latency spikes under loss, while HTTP/3 over QUIC isolates stream loss.
